row: | | Shaw et al., *Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations* (NAACL 2018): a learned vector per query–key offset, clipped at *k*, added to keys and values; on WMT14 En→De the big Transformer went from 27.9 to 29.2 BLEU (En→Fr 41.2 → 41.5) at a 7% drop in steps per second, adding sinusoidal positions back gave nothing, and BLEU was flat for any *k* ≥ 2; longer inputs not tested | [1803.02155](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02155) | ✓ [shaw-2018-self-attention-relative-position-representations.pdf](sources/shaw-2018-self-attention-relative-position-representations.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |

| | Al-Rfou et al., *Character-Level Language Modeling with Deeper Self-Attention* (AAAI 2019): a 64-layer, 235M-parameter byte-level transformer with auxiliary losses at every layer reached 1.06 bits per byte on enwik8 (512-byte context), but on lm1b its word perplexity of 40.6 trailed a word-level model's 23.7 | [1808.04444](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04444) | ✓ [alrfou-2019-character-level-language-modeling-deeper.pdf](sources/alrfou-2019-character-level-language-modeling-deeper.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

| | Kudo & Richardson, *SentencePiece* (EMNLP 2018 demo): trains subwords on raw sentences, encoding spaces as ▁ so detokenization is lossless; on KFTT Japanese→English an 8k shared-vocabulary GNMT scored 29.55 BLEU against 28.24 for an 80k word model (29.85 with pre-tokenization, so skipping the pre-tokenizer cost nothing there; on English→Japanese it helped, 21.62 vs 20.86) | [1808.06226](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226) | ✓ [kudo-2018-sentencepiece.pdf](sources/kudo-2018-sentencepiece.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

row: | | Dhariwal et al., *Jukebox: A Generative Model for Music* (2020 ⚑): autoregressive transformers over hierarchical VQ-VAE audio codes, a 5B top-level prior plus 1B upsamplers; generating one minute of top-level tokens took about an hour and upsampling it another ~8 hours, "fast parallel evaluation of likelihood but slow autoregressive sampling" | [2005.00341](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00341) | ✓ [dhariwal-2020-jukebox.pdf](sources/dhariwal-2020-jukebox.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#prefill-decode-and-the-kv-cache) |

row: | | Likhomanenko et al., *CAPE: Continuous Augmented Positional Embeddings* (NeurIPS 2021): randomly shifting and scaling absolute sinusoidal positions in training; a ViT trained at 224² and tested at 672² kept 73.4% ImageNet top-1 vs 72.2% learned absolute and 70.7% sinusoidal; on WMT14 En→De it tied relative positions (27.89 vs 27.92 BLEU), though relative positions still won at positions beyond those seen in training; no language-model test | [2106.03143](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03143) | ✓ [likhomanenko-2021-cape.pdf](sources/likhomanenko-2021-cape.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |
doubts: Note says relative positions did best 'on long test sentences'; the paper's evidence is per-position loss for positions >200 (Fig. 8) on En→De, with CAPE closing the gap on En→Fr. Close enough to leave.

row: | | Bowman, *Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models* (Critical AI 2024; arXiv 2023-04): survey; point 8 argues instruction following "isn't inherent to the model, but rather is grafted onto it using highly imperfect tools", so a model that fails a request often succeeds once it is reworded and one failure is not evidence a capability is missing; argument from cited work, no new experiments | [2304.00612](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.00612) | ✓ [bowman-2023-eight-things-know-about-large.pdf](sources/bowman-2023-eight-things-know-about-large.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#what-a-base-model-is-not) |

row: | | Yu et al., *MEGABYTE: Predicting Million-byte Sequences with Multiscale Transformers* (NeurIPS 2023): a large global model over 8-byte patches plus a small local model inside each; after 400B bytes of PG-19 at equal compute it reached test word perplexity 36.4 against 69.4 for a plain byte transformer (subword SOTA 26.5–36.3, not compute-matched) | [2305.07185](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07185) | ✓ [yu-2023-megabyte.pdf](sources/yu-2023-megabyte.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#tokens) |

| | Kazemnejad et al., *The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers* (NoPE, NeurIPS 2023): ~107M decoders trained from scratch on ten reasoning tasks with instance lengths up to 20 and tested up to 40; NoPE ranked first (MRR 0.69) ahead of T5 relative bias (0.55), ALiBi (0.50), rotary (0.33) and absolute (0.22); at 1.3B on code (1,024 context) NoPE and ALiBi held to ~1,600 tokens and blew up by 1,800 while rotary failed at 1,400; no large-scale pretraining comparison | [2305.19466](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19466) | ✓ [kazemnejad-2023-impact-positional-encoding-length-generalization.pdf](sources/kazemnejad-2023-impact-positional-encoding-length-generalization.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |

edits.old: Training sequences were up to 20 tokens long, and test sequences up to twice that.
edits.new: Training instances had a task length of up to 20 (20 words to copy, say), and test instances up to twice that.
edits.why: p.4 §3: lengths are task-instance lengths sampled from U(1, L=20) (e.g. number of words/digits), test from U(1, 2L); not token counts.

edits.old: On long files, rotary's perplexity jumps from 3.3 at 1,200 tokens to 156 at 1,400. NoPE and ALiBi are still near their in-range values at 1,600 (3.8 and 3.7)
edits.new: On files of 2,750–3,000 tokens, rotary's perplexity jumps from 3.3 at 1,200 tokens to 156 at 1,400. NoPE and ALiBi are still in single digits at 1,600 (3.8 and 3.7, against about 2.7 at 1,024)
edits.why: App. F Table 3: the quoted numbers are the [2750, 3000] length bucket only; in-range perplexity there is 2.67 (NoPE) / 2.74 (ALiBi), so 3.8/3.7 is ~40% higher, not 'near' in-range.

row: | | Graves et al., *Bayesian Flow Networks* (2023 ⚑): generation steps set independently of sequence length; on text8 (256-character sequences) it reached 1.41 bits per character at 1,000 steps and 1.43 at 100 (upper bounds), against 1.23 for an autoregressive transformer baseline | [2308.07037](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07037) | ✓ [graves-2023-bayesian-flow-networks.pdf](sources/graves-2023-bayesian-flow-networks.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#prefill-decode-and-the-kv-cache) |

row: | | Pal et al., *Giraffe: Adventures in Expanding Context Lengths in LLMs* (2023 ⚑): LLaMA-13B (trained at 2k) fine-tuned at 4,096 with linear interpolation ×16 fell on LongChat-Lines key–value retrieval from 0.64 at 2.5k to 0.10 at 16k and 0 at 17.5k, short of the naive 32k; linear scaling beat xPos, randomized positions and power/truncated bases; doubling the scale zero-shot at evaluation doubled usable context for fine-tuning scales 1 and 4 but not 16; perplexity ranked methods differently from the tasks | [2308.10882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10882) | ✓ [pal-2023-giraffe.pdf](sources/pal-2023-giraffe.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |

edits.old: Running a model at about twice the scale it was fine-tuned at doubled its usable context, with some loss of accuracy; beyond that it broke.
edits.new: Running a model at twice the scale it was fine-tuned at doubled its usable context, with some loss of accuracy, for models fine-tuned at scale 1 or 4 but not 16; beyond twice, it broke.
edits.why: §5.2 and Table 4 caption: the 2x zero-shot gain holds 'for train lengths 1 and 4 (for train length 16, it does not)'; >2x (e.g. 4x) leads to failure.

doubts: No venue found; arXiv-only, treated as preprint (note already says preprint).

row: | | Peng et al., *YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models* (ICLR 2024): NTK-by-parts interpolation plus an attention temperature √(1/t) = 0.1 ln(s) + 1; Llama 2 7B fine-tuned 400 steps at *s* = 16 on 64k PG19 chunks (~0.1% of pretraining data), then 200 more at *s* = 32, reached sliding-window perplexity 2.37 at 128k on Proof-pile and >99% passkey retrieval, with MMLU 43.8 → 41.7; untuned on LLaMA 7B (2k) it held 3.45 at 32k where PI exceeded 100 | [2309.00071](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00071) | ✓ [peng-2023-yarn.pdf](sources/peng-2023-yarn.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |

edits.new: With *s* = 32 (200 more steps from the *s* = 16 checkpoint, still on 64k chunks) the model reached
edits.why: §4.1 and Table 1: the 400-step run is the s=16 model; the s=32 model that reached 2.37 at 128k was trained 400+200 steps, continuing from the s=16 checkpoint.

doubts: Ledger venue is null. The local PDF is arXiv v3 (Feb 2026) without a venue header; YaRN was published at ICLR 2024 (note already cites it as ICLR 2024). Coordinator may want to confirm and set the ledger venue.

row: | | He & Hofmann, *Simplifying Transformer Blocks* (ICLR 2024): removing skip connections, value and output projections and sequential sub-blocks (with identity-biased attention) matched Pre-LN per-step training on a 100M-class GPT (CodeParrot) and Crammed BERT; in BERT the blocks used 16% fewer parameters (101M vs 120M) for up to 16% higher throughput at equal GLUE; dropping norms too slowed per-step training slightly and gave NaNs in fine-tuning; only 100–300M models tested | [2311.01906](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01906) | ✓ [he-2023-simplifying-transformer-blocks.pdf](sources/he-2023-simplifying-transformer-blocks.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#the-transformer-block-and-the-gpt-stack) |

headings.heading: The transformer block and the GPT stack

edits.old: Their GPT trained as fast per step as a Pre-LN one, with 16% fewer parameters and 16% higher throughput.
edits.new: Their simplified GPT trained as fast per step as a Pre-LN one, and in a BERT model the same blocks used 16% fewer parameters (101M vs 120M) for up to 16% higher throughput.
edits.why: §5 Table 1: the 16% parameter and 16% throughput figures are measured on Crammed BERT (masked LM), not on the GPT/CodeParrot runs; abstract gives 15% fewer params, Table 1 101M vs 120M (16%).
